title: What skills are and how to build on other people's work
intro: Almost everything you explain to the AI every morning can be saved so you never have to repeat it again, and almost everything you want to build already exists half-built somewhere. By the end you'll know how to turn a procedure of yours into a skill the AI loads on its own when it's needed, and how to start a project by copying someone else's instead of staring at a blank screen.

theory.title: A skill is a recipe the AI pulls out of its own pocket
theory.text: A skill is a short document with one of your procedures saved in it: how you draft a quote at your business, what fields your customer form has, how you respond to a complaint. You write it once and it stays there. The good part isn't that it's saved — it's that the AI opens it on its own when it sees it's needed: you write "prepare the quote for the folks at the shop", it recognizes what's going on, goes and finds your recipe, and follows it. You don't have to remember anything or paste instructions every time.
theory.analogy: It's the folder of plastic sleeves the bar manager keeps behind the counter. Nobody memorizes how the register gets closed on Sundays: you pull out the sheet, follow it, and put it back.

theory.title: A skill isn't memory, and that difference saves you headaches
theory.text: The AI's memory stores facts about you: that you live in a certain city, that your company is called such-and-such. A skill stores steps, not facts. Memory kicks in somewhat randomly; a skill kicks in when what you're asking matches what its description says. That's why the first line of a skill, the "this is used when...", is the single most important part of the whole document. Describe it poorly and you'll have a perfect recipe that never gets opened.

theory.title: It's created by dictating it, not by writing it yourself
theory.text: You don't have to draft anything. You tell the AI the procedure the same way you'd explain it to someone new starting at your job, quirks and exceptions included, and ask it to turn that into an instructions document. It hands you back the organized text and you paste it wherever your app keeps these things. In Claude they're called Skills; in ChatGPT it's a custom GPT or a Project with instructions; in Gemini it's called a Gem. The name and the button change, the idea stays the same.

theory.title: A repository is a folder with memory
theory.text: GitHub is the storehouse where project material lives: the files and the log of who changed what and when. Each project occupies a repository, which is that folder with history. There are millions of them and most are public: you go in, look around, and take a copy without asking permission or paying. Watch out for the word public when you're the one creating the repository: whatever you put in there, anyone can read it, including any passwords you accidentally leave in it.
theory.analogy: It's a photocopier open to the public with a sign-in book next to it: anyone can walk off with a copy, and everyone can see who touched what.

theory.title: The template is the button that copies someone else's work
theory.text: Some repositories are marked as templates. On their page, above the file list and next to the green "Code" button, there's another one that says "Use this template". Click it and GitHub creates you a clean copy inside your own account, under your name and without the author's history: a whole project, already built, that from that second on is yours. If a repository isn't marked as a template, the equivalent is "Fork", which also gives you a copy, but it carries the history along and stays linked back to the original.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between commissioning a house from an architect and buying a pre-designed one from a catalog: you get it built either way, but you just pick the kitchen color.

theory.title: How to tell in thirty seconds if a template is worth it
theory.text: Three things, in this order. The date of the last change, shown to the right of the file list: if it says three years ago, keep moving, because half the pieces no longer match today's. The stars, up at the top: they're GitHub's "likes", and below two hundred you're usually the guinea pig. And the license, in the right-hand column: MIT and Apache 2.0 mean you can use it even to make money from it; if it says AGPL, or nothing at all, ask before you build a business on top of it.

tasks.title: Find where your app stores procedures
tasks.where: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, ideally opened in your computer's browser
tasks.action: In Claude: click your name in the bottom left, go into Settings, and look for the Capabilities or Skills section. In ChatGPT: in the left column click "GPTs" or "Explore GPTs" and then the create button. In Gemini: in the left column click "Gems" and then "New Gem". For now just look, don't create anything yet.
tasks.expect: An empty form with two boxes: a small one for the name and description, and a large one that says Instructions. That's the mold for your future skill.
tasks.stuck: If those options don't show up, it's usually one of two things: you're in the mobile app, or you're on the free plan. Open it on a computer; if it's still not there, keep going with the rest of the guide, the templates section doesn't need it.

tasks.title: Dictate the procedure you repeat every week
tasks.where: In your AI's text box, in a normal conversation
tasks.action: Pick something you always do the same way: a quote, a follow-up email, the Monday summary. Tell the AI about it using the text below, swapping the example for your own. Don't hold back on details or on the odd exceptions: whatever you leave out, it will make up.
tasks.prompt: I want to turn a procedure of mine into a skill, meaning an instructions document you load on your own when it's needed. Here's the procedure: [describe it here in your own way, out of order is fine]. Before writing anything, ask me five questions to catch the details I'm leaving out. Then write me the document in English with three parts: a first line saying when this is used, the steps in order, and what should never be done.
tasks.expect: First the five questions. Once you answer them, a document about half a screen long, with the "when this is used" line at the top and the numbered steps below.
tasks.stuck: If it jumps straight into writing without asking, reply: "You skipped the questions. Ask me the five before writing anything."

tasks.title: Save that text as a skill
tasks.where: In the panel you found in the first task
tasks.action: Copy the document the AI gave you. Go back to the panel, click the create button, give it a short, recognizable name ("Shop quotes"), paste the first line into the description field and everything else into the instructions field. Save.
tasks.expect: The skill shows up in your list with its name. There's usually a toggle to turn it on or off: leave it on.
tasks.stuck: If the description field has little room, boil it down to one sentence using the words you actually use: "Used when I ask for a quote for a shop customer." That's enough.

tasks.title: Test the skill without naming it
tasks.where: In a new conversation with your AI
tasks.action: Open a new chat, and make sure it's genuinely new, so it doesn't carry over what you talked about before. Ask for the task the way you'd ask a coworker, without saying the word skill or the name you gave it.
tasks.prompt: Prepare the quote for the new customer: clutch replacement, 2016 car, delivery in four days.
tasks.expect: The answer comes back already in your format, following your steps, without you having pasted anything. In some apps you'll see a line at the top saying which skill was used. If the result matches what you got when pasting the instructions by hand, it worked.
tasks.stuck: If the answer is generic, the problem is in the description, not the steps. Rewrite that first line using the exact words you use when asking for it: quote, customer, shop.

tasks.title: Fix the skill using the very answer that went wrong
tasks.where: In your AI app, in the same chat where it failed
tasks.action: When the result comes out wrong, don't rewrite the skill from memory. Show it the mistake and ask for the entire corrected document, because if it gives you only the piece, you'll end up with a text full of patches.
tasks.prompt: This answer of yours doesn't work because of this: [say what's wrong, with examples]. Rewrite the complete instructions document fixing that, and tell me in one line what you changed. Give me the whole thing to paste, not just the fragment.
tasks.expect: The complete document again, with the fix inside, and one line explaining what it touched. You paste it over the old one in the panel and save.
tasks.stuck: If the same mistake happens twice, that step is written as a suggestion instead of a rule. Ask it: "Write that step as a rule that can't be interpreted two different ways."

tasks.title: Go into GitHub and look up the templates on the list
tasks.action: If you don't have an account, click "Sign up" in the top right: it asks for an email, a password, and a username. It's free, no card required, and that name is public and shows up in front of everything you do, so pick something presentable. Then use the search box at the top and paste the full name, slash included. Here's the short list, with what each does and when it's useful. — anthropics/skills: Anthropic's official skills, already written (filling out a Word doc, building an Excel file, generating a PDF). Use it to copy the style of a well-written skill before writing your own. — anthropics/anthropic-quickstarts: small, complete projects, like a customer support assistant or a data analyst. Use it when you want something that works from day one. — vercel/ai-chatbot: an AI chat with its own website, user accounts, and history, ready to publish. Use it if your idea is an assistant for your customers with its own website. — vercel/commerce: an entire online store, with catalog, cart, and checkout. Use it if you sell products and don't want to build the store from scratch. — shadcn-ui/ui: not a project, it's a kit of interface pieces (buttons, forms, tables) that look great. Use it once you already have the site and want it to stop looking like a school project. — openai/openai-cookbook: hundreds of worked examples of things you can do with AI. Use it when you're not sure if what you want is even possible. — f/awesome-chatgpt-prompts: a huge list of already-tested instructions, organized by profession. Use it to steal a starting point instead of fighting a blank page. — n8n-io/self-hosted-ai-starter-kit: a set of AI automations already wired together. Use it if your idea is for this to run itself every morning. — vercel.com/templates: this isn't GitHub but a gallery, with hundreds of templates that come with a "Deploy" button that creates the repository and publishes the site in one shot. Use it if you want something of yours online today. — astro.build/themes: blog, portfolio, and business website templates, nice-looking and lightweight. Use it if what you're showing is your work, not an app with user accounts.
tasks.expect: Each project's page: the file list at the top with the date of the last change and the star count, and below it a long text, usually in English, explaining it. Note the links for the two or three that fit what you need.
tasks.stuck: If the search returns a thousand similar results, you probably typed only the second half of the name. Paste the full name with the slash: vercel/ai-chatbot, not ai-chatbot.

tasks.title: Get a verdict on the template before falling for it
tasks.where: In your AI's text box, with the project link copied
tasks.action: That long text under the file list is called the README and it's the project's manual. Don't translate it yourself: hand it to the AI and ask it to also tell you the downsides.
tasks.prompt: Here's the link to a GitHub project: [paste the link]. Tell me, plainly and without jargon: 1) exactly what it does, 2) what I'd need to have set up for it to work and roughly how much that would cost me per month, 3) whether it fits this: [describe your idea in one sentence], 4) which three files I'd need to change to adapt it, 5) the biggest reason I shouldn't use it. If you can't verify something, say so instead of assuming.
tasks.expect: Five numbered answers, with number 5 being a real downside. If number 2 turns up paid services you weren't expecting (a database, an AI key), better to find out now than after two afternoons of work.
tasks.stuck: If it says it can't open the link, go to the project page yourself, scroll down to the long text, select it, copy it, and paste it into the chat.

tasks.title: Copy the project into your own account
tasks.where: On github.com, on the page of the project you picked
tasks.action: Above the file list, look for the green "Use this template" button and choose "Create a new repository". Name your copy in lowercase with hyphens, no accents or spaces: shop-quotes. Right below it asks Public or Private: choose Private while you're learning, because public means anyone can read whatever you put inside. Click "Create repository". If that green button doesn't exist, use "Fork" in the top right: for what you need, it does the same thing.
tasks.expect: In a few seconds, a page identical to the original but with your username in front of the project's name. Those files are now yours and you can wreck them without worry.
tasks.stuck: If it says the name is already taken, you have another repository with the same name; add a number at the end and continue.

tasks.title: Ask for the change plan before touching a single file
tasks.action: A template comes with the original author's text, colors, and name. Before diving in and changing things at random, have it give you the list and the order.
tasks.prompt: I've copied the [project name] template to my GitHub account. My idea is this: [three sentences: what it is, who it's for, and what it needs to do]. Give me the list of changes in the order they should be made, starting with the most visible (name, text, colors) and leaving for last whatever might break something. For each change, tell me which file it's in, what text to search for, and what to replace it with. Not a single untranslated word left over.
tasks.expect: An ordered list with specific file names and the exact text to replace. If it gives you forty steps, ask it: "give me just the first ten".
tasks.stuck: If it gives you instructions starting with opening a terminal, reply: "I don't have a terminal and don't want to use one. Tell me how to do it from the GitHub website, editing the files with the pencil icon."

tasks.title: Change the first piece of text right from GitHub's website
tasks.action: Click through the file list until you reach the file the AI pointed to. Above the content, on the right, there's a pencil icon: click it, find the English phrase, and type yours over it. At the bottom, click "Commit changes" and confirm in the small window that pops up. Every save gets logged with a date and author, so if you mess up, you can always go back: nothing is ever permanently lost here.
tasks.expect: The file with your sentence in it and, at the top, a notice of the latest change with a timestamp from moments ago.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the pencil, you're probably looking at the original author's project and not yours. Check that your username shows up in front of the project name at the top.

tasks.title: Publish your copy on the internet without opening a terminal
tasks.action: Go to vercel.com, click "Sign up", and choose "Continue with GitHub". It'll ask you to authorize the connection: on that screen you can grant it access only to the repository you just created instead of to all of them, which is recommended. Then click "Add New" and then "Project", find your repository in the list, click "Import", and "Deploy". Wait a minute or two. The free plan is called Hobby, costs $0, and doesn't ask for a card, but it's for personal projects, not for selling things. From here on, the loop is set up: you change a file in GitHub and Vercel republishes the site on its own in under a minute.
tasks.expect: A celebration screen with an address like shop-quotes.vercel.app. Click it and there's your website working, with someone else's project and your own text.
tasks.stuck: If the deployment finishes red, copy the error text and paste it to the AI with this: "This failed while publishing on Vercel. Tell me in plain English which file to change and what to write." Nine times out of ten it's a missing key or setting, not something actually broken.

tasks.title: Turn your project into a template for your future self
tasks.where: On github.com, inside your repository, on the Settings tab
tasks.action: Once you have something working and suspect you'll repeat it for another client, go into your repository, click "Settings" in the top row of tabs, and check the "Template repository" box in the first section. Before checking it, go through and make sure no password or key was left inside the files, especially if the repository is public.
tasks.expect: Back on the repository's main page, the green "Use this template" button shows up next to "Code". From there, setting up the next project the same way takes ten seconds.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the checkbox, make sure you're in the repository's Settings and not your account's: the repository's settings are inside the project, on the same row as Code, Issues, and Pull requests.

canDo: Save a procedure of yours once and have the AI apply it on its own every time the topic comes up
Fix that skill on the spot when something goes wrong, using the very answer that failed
Start a website, a store, or an assistant from a project that already works, without writing anything from scratch
Tell in five minutes whether a template fits, whether it's still maintained, and whether it'll cost you money
Change text and publish on the internet using only the browser
Turn your setup into a template to reuse for the next client
cantDo: A skill doesn't learn on its own: if the procedure changes at your business, you change it by hand
Skills don't travel between apps: the one you write for Claude has to be pasted again into ChatGPT or Gemini
A template doesn't guess your business; it saves you the skeleton, not the decisions
Copying the repository doesn't copy the paid services it relies on underneath (a database, AI keys): you set those up yourself separately
Vercel's free plan can't handle a business with real traffic; it's built for personal projects
No template exempts you from checking the license if you're going to charge for the result
Deleting a repository on GitHub can't be undone: it takes the files and the entire history with it
words: Skill
A short document with one of your procedures saved in it, which the AI opens on its own when what you're asking matches its description.
Gem / custom GPT
What skills are called in Gemini and in ChatGPT. Same idea, different button.
Repository (repo)
A project's folder on GitHub, with all its files and the log of who changed what and when.
Template (template repository)
A repository marked so that anyone can get a clean copy with one button, without carrying the author's history.
Fork
The other way to copy someone else's project: it also brings it into your account, but it carries the history along and stays linked back to the original.
README
The long text under the file list that explains what the project is and how to get it running. Almost always in English; ask the AI to translate it for you.
Commit
Every time you save a change, a snapshot gets stored with a date and author. That's why you can always go back.
License
The document that says what you're allowed to do with someone else's work. MIT and Apache 2.0 are free-for-all, including for making money. No license means it's not yours to use.
Stars
GitHub's "likes". They give you a sense of how many people have been through here before you.
Deploy
Taking the files from your repository to a server on the internet so the website can be seen from outside your own computer.
